expert_decision.reason: Nakamura (2012, 10.1515/iral-2012-0001) conducts a 2 x 2 x 2 factorial experiment with 72 Japanese EFL learners testing three factors: skewed vs. balanced verb frequency (Casenhiser & Goldberg, 2005), pronoun input consistency in the noun phrase slots (Childers & Tomasello, 2001), and presentation order of high-frequency verbs (Goldberg, Casenhiser, & White, 2007). For Childers & Tomasello (2001, 'The role of pronouns in young children’s acquisition of the English transitive construction', Developmental Psychology 37, 739–748; DOI 10.1037/0012-1649.37.6.739), Hypothesis 2 explicitly tests whether the positive main effect of pronoun input consistency found by Childers & Tomasello (2001) holds in L2 construction learning, with dedicated empirical results in Section 6.3 ('Effects of input consistency') and discussion in Section 8.2 ('Input consistency'). Only Casenhiser & Goldberg (2005, input_row_index 299) is in the shipped rows; Childers & Tomasello (2001) is a distinct primary empirical study missing from the shipped dataset. Prior adjudication and state files do not exist for this item.

expert_decision.location: Section 4 (Purpose and hypotheses of the present study), Hypothesis 3 & Hypothesis 5; Sections 6.4–6.5; Sections 8.3–8.4, line 1
expert_decision.quote: Goldberg et al. (2007) showed that initially providing skewed input facilitated rapid construction generalization. The present study investigates this effect for the position of verbs with relative high token frequency. Relative here denotes that the high token frequency of verbs is adjusted for the experimental groups (four times for +the skewed group or twice for the −skewed group). We expect significant positive effects for the forward order of frequent verbs and positive main effects for order of frequent verbs.
expert_decision.reason: In the same 2 x 2 x 2 factorial experiment (Nakamura, 2012, 10.1515/iral-2012-0001), the third experimental factor directly tests the presentation order finding of Goldberg, Casenhiser, & White (2007, 'Constructions as categories of language: The role of order on construction learning', New Ideas in Psychology 25, 70–86), comparing learners exposed to high-frequency exemplar verbs first (+first / forward order) versus last (-first / backward order). Hypothesis 3 and Hypothesis 5 formulate direct empirical predictions based on Goldberg et al. (2007), which are empirically tested in Section 6.4 ('Effects of order of frequent verbs') and Section 6.5 ('Effects of interaction of variables') and evaluated in Sections 8.3 and 8.4 ('This result is consistent with the finding of Goldberg et al. (2007)'). While Casenhiser & Goldberg (2005, input_row_index 299) is in the shipped rows and tested via Hypothesis 1 (skewed vs. balanced input), Goldberg, Casenhiser, & White (2007) reports a separate primary experiment manipulating exemplar presentation order and is absent from the shipped dataset (as well as distinct from target_index 1, Childers & Tomasello, 2001). Prior adjudication and state files do not exist for this item.
